name: Right to Be Forgotten
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Erasing a Record That Was Built Never to Change
lesson.summary: The GDPR's right to erasure gives individuals a legal right to have personal data deleted, a right that collides directly with blockchain immutability, and the practical industry response is to keep personal data off-chain and put only a hash or pointer on the ledger.
lesson.body:
The whole design point of a blockchain, established in Immutability, is that once a block is validated and added, changing it would require rewriting every subsequent block and getting the majority of the network's computing power or stake to accept the rewrite, something intentionally made close to impossible. That property is exactly what gives blockchain records their trustworthiness, since no one can quietly go back and alter history. It is also exactly what makes deletion structurally difficult.

The EU's General Data Protection Regulation, in Article 17, gives individuals a legal right to erasure, commonly called the right to be forgotten. On request, an organization holding someone's personal data generally must delete it. This creates a well documented, genuinely unresolved tension: if personal data such as a name, an email address, or biometric information is written directly onto a public blockchain, no participant has the unilateral ability to erase it, since doing so would mean rewriting a shared history that potentially thousands of independent nodes worldwide have already validated and stored copies of. European data protection authorities and legal scholars have been wrestling publicly with this exact conflict since GDPR took effect in 2018, and there is no single settled resolution. Different regulators and courts have taken different positions on how strictly the presence of a hash or pointer counts as personal data under the law.

The workaround that has actually become common practice, and that connects directly back to Hybrid Architecture, is to never put personal data on-chain in the first place. The actual personal data is stored off-chain in an ordinary, deletable database or file store that a specific accountable organization controls, and only a cryptographic hash, essentially a fingerprint, of that data is written to the blockchain. The hash lets anyone verify that a given piece of off-chain data has not been tampered with, without the chain ever holding the sensitive content itself. Crucially, if an individual later exercises their right to erasure, the organization deletes the underlying data from its off-chain store. The hash remains on the blockchain forever, but a hash of deleted data cannot be reversed back into the original personal information, so what is left on-chain becomes, for practical purposes, meaningless, a fingerprint with nothing left for it to identify or match against.

It is worth being precise about the limits of this workaround rather than overselling it. The on-chain hash is still permanently and technically present, and some data protection authorities and legal analyses have raised the question of whether a hash of personal data should itself count as personal data under GDPR's broad definition, particularly if it could ever be linked back to an individual through other means. There is ongoing legal debate rather than a single settled answer, and this connects to the broader tension covered in Regulatory Compliance and Data Sovereignty: a technology's core property of immutability and replication runs headlong into a legal right that assumes data can always be found and deleted. A handful of more exotic technical proposals, such as chameleon hash schemes that allow a specific authorized party to modify certain blocks under tightly controlled conditions, or permissioned ledgers where a known operator can prune old records, exist to address this more directly, but they trade away some of the very immutability that makes a blockchain trustworthy in the first place. That tradeoff is the theme running through this entire chapter batch: there is rarely a free lunch, only a series of explicit choices between competing properties that have to be made deliberately.
